newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Giant Russian aluminium smelter sees higher output.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Giant Russian aluminium smelter sees higher output.

text.p: Bigger is better says the management of the world's largest aluminium smelter, which has begun an expansion programme but has generally turned up its nose at totally modernising its smoke-blackened plant.

The 30-year old aluminium smelter, a Soviet-era creation which belches smoke over Siberia's pine forests, exports about 600,000 tonnes of primary aluminium around the world from more than 20 workshops, each some 500 metres (yards) long.
General Director Boris Gromov said Bratsk had finished five percent of a three-year, 50 billion rouble ($9.3 million) plan to bring output back up to the Soviet-era record of 857,000 tonnes.
"We want to return to our peak production," he told a recent news conference, predicting aluminium output would be back at 857,000 tonnes by 1998 or 1999, climbing slowly from 772,500 tonnes in 1995.
Sooty murals heralding socialism and world peace decorate the factory, powered by cheap electricity from the Bratsk hydro plant, one of the world's most powerful.
Bratsk closed down one production line in the early 1990s because it was not cost-efficient. Environmental organisation Greenpeace said the smelter was a major polluter.

Officials acknowledge that the environment suffers. Pine trees in a 60 sq km (25 sq mile) "sanitary zone" around the plant are damaged by unsufficiently filtered exhaust gases which officials say blow away from the nearby city of Bratsk.
But the workers, sheathed in thick cotton smocks and face masks, are paid on time -- a triumph for the company in a country where millions of workers have to wait months for their money.
Production has declined but Gromov said modernisation of the now closed production line, using company profits, will bring output back on track.
He said additional financing from commercial bank loans and new share issues was possible.
But many officials at AOOT Bratsky Aluminievy Zavod (BrAZ) see improved efficiency, not technology, as the road to success.
Production department head Eduard Lasyenko said output of Bratsk's staple, A7 grade 99.7 percent pure aluminium, was currently about 60 percent of production, up some 10 percent on levels a year ago.
"There is a lot of hands-on work in our workshops. Quality depends on the experience of workers and the condition of the equipment," he told Reuters.
The plant uses labour-intensive technology and officials say a major overhaul of the smelting process cannot be profitable.

Lasyenko predicted A7 output would rise to 70 or 80 percent of total production in two years, but he said improvements, such as automatic alumina pumps to feed the raw material into electrolysis smelters, "still need work".
The company says the long shops, where spurts of flame periodically break through white alumina powder ready for roasting in the smelters, are improving step by step.
"Our indicators get better and better. And if this old lady is getting better, then it's not such an old lady," said Bratsk deputy director for economics and strategic planning, Yuri Purdenko.
"We have the most efficient factory, though others may have more modern equipment."
Sayansk Aluminium, a relatively modern plant also in Siberia, which can produce higher grade product has approximately the same electrical efficiency, he said.
"We closed down a shop for higher-quality aluminium because it was less effective." Bratsk has closed its single workshop producing 99.99 percent pure aluminium.

Bratsk officials vary in their estimates of electric efficiency. Purdenko said Bratsk uses about 18,000 kilowatt hours to produce a tonne of aluminium, and Lasenko said the average was about 16,500 kilowatt hours.
Bratsk 1995 pretax profit rose to 1.19 trillion roubles from 401 billion roubles in 1994.
The firm will stick to primary aluminium production instead of adding lines for finished products, such as aluminium cans.

Gromov predicted domestic demand for finished products will rise as the Russian economy improves. Bratsk wants to send aluminium to local suppliers who will meet this demand, so firm exports could decline from the current 600,000 tonnes per year.
But he said Bratsk would reach finished-product markets through Siberian Aluminium, a financial industrial group allying aluminium and alumina producers and financiers.
Siberian Aluminium includes Bratsk, Sayansk Aluminium, Pavlodar Aluminium, Britain's Trans-World Metals Group and others. ($1=5384 Rouble)
